details:
**Anselm's ontological argument (Proslogion)**
St. Anselm of Canterbury's Proslogion (c. 1078) defines God as "that than which nothing greater can be conceived." It argues that a being existing in reality is greater than one existing only in the understanding, so God must exist in reality. It is the first and most famous ontological argument, meaning an argument for God's existence from the concept of God alone.

**Gaunilo's "lost island" (On Behalf of the Fool)**
The monk Gaunilo of Marmoutiers replied to Anselm with a parody, a reductio ad absurdum. By the same reasoning, he argued, one could prove that a perfect "lost island," more excellent than all others, must exist. His title refers to the fool of Psalms 14:1 and 53:1, who "hath said in his heart, There is no God."

**Aquinas's Five Ways (Summa Theologica)**
In the Summa Theologica, Thomas Aquinas rejected Anselm's ontological argument and gave five proofs of God's existence. They argue from motion (the "unmoved" or "first mover," borrowed from Aristotle's prime mover), from efficient causation (the "first cause"), from contingency, from degrees of perfection, and from the ordered design of the world (the teleological argument). In the same work he also answers the objection that the existence of evil disproves God.

**Russell's teapot**
Bertrand Russell imagined a china teapot orbiting the Sun between Earth and Mars, too small to be detected by telescopes. He argued that the burden of proof lies on the person making an unfalsifiable claim, not on the doubter. Russell also argued for atheism in his 1927 Battersea Town Hall lecture "Why I Am Not a Christian," where he said religion rests mainly on fear.

**Pascal's Wager (Pensées)**
In his posthumously published Pensées (1670), Blaise Pascal argued that believing in God is the rational bet. If God exists, the believer gains infinitely (eternal life) and the unbeliever risks infinite loss (damnation). If God does not exist, either party loses only a finite amount.

**"God is dead" (Nietzsche)**
Friedrich Nietzsche's famous declaration, most memorably spoken by the madman in The Gay Science. The madman says "we have killed him" and asks "What festivals of atonement, what sacred games shall we have to invent?", which expresses Nietzsche's worry about the loss of meaning that would follow the collapse of belief in God.

**"Existence is not a predicate" (Kant)**
Immanuel Kant's objection to the ontological argument in the Critique of Pure Reason. He argued that existence does not add anything to the concept of a thing, so it cannot be one of the perfections that a supremely perfect being must have.

**Modal ontological arguments (Plantinga, Hartshorne, Gödel)**
These 20th-century versions use modal logic. In The Nature of Necessity, Alvin Plantinga used the S5 system to give a "victorious" argument that if a maximally great being is possible, it exists in all possible worlds. Charles Hartshorne defended a modal version against Kant's objection. Kurt Gödel wrote a formal ontological proof, which Jordan Howard Sobel criticized for leading to "modal collapse," the conclusion that every truth is necessary.

**Watchmaker analogy (William Paley)**
William Paley's teleological argument, or argument from design. Just as finding a watch implies a watchmaker, the complex design of nature implies a divine designer. Richard Dawkins's "Ultimate Boeing 747 gambit" is a modern argument against design reasoning of this kind.

**Kalam cosmological argument (al-Ghazali, William Lane Craig)**
This argument holds that whatever begins to exist has a cause, the universe began to exist, and therefore the universe has a cause. It was developed in medieval Islamic theology by al-Ghazali, whose Incoherence of the Philosophers attacks the philosophers' inability to prove God's existence. William Lane Craig revived it, and he also argues from the "fine-tuning" of the universe.

**Problem of evil**
This is the classic argument against God's existence: how can an omnipotent, omniscient, and omnibenevolent God allow suffering? Hume asked "Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? Then is he impotent," and William Rowe pointed to a fawn dying slowly in a forest fire. Responses include Augustine's view of evil as a privation of good, Leibniz's Theodicy ("best of all possible worlds"), John Hick's "soul-making" theodicy, and Alvin Plantinga's Free Will Defense, which uses the idea of "transworld depravity."

**Descartes's Meditations (Third and Fifth)**
In the Third Meditation, René Descartes argues that his idea of an infinite, perfect God could only have been caused by God himself (the "trademark" argument). In the Fifth Meditation, he gives his own ontological argument, saying that God's existence is as inseparable from God's essence as three angles are from a triangle, and that God has a "true and immutable nature."

**Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion**
David Hume's posthumously published dialogue, in which three characters debate the existence and nature of God. Cleanthes defends the design argument, Demea defends an a priori cosmological argument and orthodox piety, and the skeptic Philo raises objections to both.

**Spinoza: "God or Nature" (Deus sive Natura)**
In his Ethics, Baruch Spinoza argued that God is the single infinite substance, with infinitely many attributes including thought and extension. He identified God with nature itself. Other early modern clues include George Berkeley, for whom God's perception keeps unperceived objects in existence, and Christian Wolff, who made God one of the three objects of special metaphysics, along with the soul and the world.

**"If God does not exist, everything is permitted"**
This idea is associated with Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov, which holds that morality collapses without God. Simone de Beauvoir rejected it in The Ethics of Ambiguity, arguing that without God humans bear even more responsibility for their actions.
